SCHOOL ROOM · THE CAFETERIA · 62 CARDS · AGES 2–5

The Cafeteria — every card carries a food on the tray.

Sixty-two foods, sixty-two little activities: point to the apple, count the peas, match the sandwich, find the water. Every card names one cafeteria food and prints one activity under its name; every food has its lesson and printable twin right here — and the room runs on the lunchroom’s oldest rule: taste a little, name a lot, try the next one tomorrow.

Open the food shelves ↓The printable set ↗
HOW THIS ROOM WORKS

Read the card. Do the tiny activity. Then lunch tastes louder.

Every card in this deck does two jobs: it names one food and it prints one activity — a pointing, counting, matching or finding game the card means literally. The short pages on this shelf show each card, quote its activity word for word, and add one way to set the food up tonight. When one food becomes a favorite, its lesson page carries the full teaching — what the food is, what the activity secretly trains, the parent script, the questions to ask — and the library page holds the printable twin with a download button.

The shelves run in file order like a real serving line: the first twenty-nine cards, apple through ham-sandwich, sit on the main shelf; the rest of the line — juice through yogurt — waits under More foods. For the foods’ naming cousins, the Fruits & Vegetables class names eight fruits and eight vegetables with their lessons right here, and the Kitchen Helper class names the tools that prepare all of it.

GAMES THE CAFETERIA PLAYS

Between courses, play.

Lunch tables run on games the way kitchens run on timers, and the school’s games shelf holds the rules for the ones this room plays best: Hot Potato passes a pretend spud round the table to real music, Simon Says turns chew-like-a-rabbit and stir-like-a-spoon into listening practice, and the Treasure Hunt hides food cards all over the room for a hungry little detective. Full rules on every page — dessert can wait.

AROUND THE SCHOOL

Where to wander next.

Explore the School — every room, one door each ↗Name the fruits & vegetables in Class 22 · Ages 3–5 ↗Meet the Kitchen Helper’s tools · Ages 3–6 ↗Eating well in Class 40 · Ages 4–5 ↗

The Cafeteria sits on the school’s room shelf beside the Library, the Garden, the Playground, the Music Room, the Art Room and the Clubs. Class 22 is its naming cousin — the fruits and vegetables this room serves — the Kitchen Helper class is its tools-and-safety twin: what chops, pours and stirs the food this room dishes out, and the Healthy Food & Eating Well class is its eating-well shelf: twenty-one food-habit cards for ages 4–5, from the balanced plate to trying new foods, for families ready to turn the tray into the table.

Tasting is the curriculum. Every activity on these cards hides real work — pointing, counting, matching, waiting — inside something the child thinks is just lunch. Name the food first; the bravery follows the spoon.

AT THE TABLE

Table manners, printed.

The Cafeteria names the food — the Manners flashcards mind the table: chew quietly, use two hands, wipe the table, offer to share. Thirty-two printable manners cards for ages 3–5, each with a how-to-practise tip, a download and a one-tap print on a single page. Print both decks and lunch gets louder in the best way.

CAFETERIA LESSON · CAFETERIA · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Apple — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson turns the apple card into a pointing game — the fastest way a two-year-old shows what they know before words arrive.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

An apple is a round fruit with a thin red or green skin, a crisp white inside and a small core of seeds in the middle. It grows on trees in every cool climate on Earth.

What does it mean?

Point to the apple asks the child to find one thing among nothing else — the simplest search there is. Pointing is how understanding shows up months before words do.

What does the child need to know?

Hold the card up, wait quietly, and let the finger do the talking. If the child grabs the card instead, that still counts: a grab is a point with enthusiasm.

Why this matters

Apples are the fruit children meet first and keep meeting — in lunchboxes, at stands, in books — so naming one pays off every single day.

What it teaches

Visual attention, hand-eye aim, and the first food word a child can carry everywhere.

Words to learn

appleredroundfruitleafcrunchy

Say this to your child

“Where is the apple? ... There it is! You pointed to the apple. Red and round — an apple. Can you tap it one more time?”

Step by step

  1. Set the card on the table and put your hands in your lap. Ask where the apple is and wait — a real wait, five full seconds. When the finger lands, celebrate once and move on: name it, tap the picture, done. Repeat at snack time with a real apple beside the card and let the child touch fruit to picture.

Look closer at the picture

Watch for the finger hovering before it lands — that hover is thinking happening in real time. Some children point with their whole hand first; a full-hand point still counts.

Ask your child

Where is the apple? What color is the apple? Is it big or little? Where is the leaf?

What your child can say or do

Apple! / Red one! / My apple. / Apple like in my bag.

Out in the real world

Apples ride in nearly every lunchbox on Earth, so the word gets practiced at home, at school and at the store — one word, three stages a day.

Try it together

Hide the card behind your back, behind a cushion, then under the table and ask where the apple went — finding it again earns the biggest point of all.

Understanding check

Cover the card and ask what the picture was. A child who says apple, points to a real apple across the room, or signs the word has passed the check.

This lesson pairs with the Apple flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Cafeteria.

CAFETERIA LESSON · CAFETERIA · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Applesauce — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson uses the applesauce card to teach texture — the apple children know, transformed into something they can stir and spoon.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Applesauce is apples cooked until soft and mashed smooth, usually with nothing else added. It is the same fruit as the apple card with the crunch taken out.

What does it mean?

Point to the applesauce asks the child to tell two lookalike cups apart — the gold cup and every other cup on the tray. Looking closely is the real skill underneath.

What does the child need to know?

Keep a real cup nearby if you can: the connection between card and cup is instant, and peeling the foil lid is a lesson in itself.

Why this matters

Soft foods are how young eaters survive new textures, and applesauce is the bridge food between milk and everything chewy.

What it teaches

Texture words, spoon control, and the idea that one food can wear two forms.

Words to learn

applesaucesoftsmoothspooncupgold

Say this to your child

“This is applesauce — apple that went soft. Feel the cup — smooth. Let us stir one slow circle... now one fast circle! Ready for a taste?”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and ask what food this is. Let the child answer freely — sauce, apple, mush are all welcome. Then show a real cup, peel the lid together and stir one slow circle before the first taste. Finish by putting the apple card and the applesauce card side by side: same fruit, two costumes.

Look closer at the picture

Watch the spoon grip: most two-year-olds fist the handle, and that is exactly right for now. The wrist rotation comes months later on its own.

Ask your child

What food is in the cup? Is it crunchy or soft? What did the apple turn into?

What your child can say or do

Sauce! / Soft one. / More applesauce. / Apple went squish.

Out in the real world

Applesauce waits in nearly every school kitchen as the gentle side dish — the food a tired or teething child can still eat happily.

Try it together

Pretend the spoon is an airplane landing in the applesauce airport — three circles in the air, one smooth landing, one passenger bite. Repeat until the cup is empty.

Understanding check

Set the apple card and the applesauce card side by side and ask which one you eat with a spoon. A correct tap — or a spoon raised at the right cup — passes.

This lesson pairs with the Applesauce flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Cafeteria.

CAFETERIA LESSON · CAFETERIA · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Bagel — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the bagel through its most interesting part — the hole — and turns a breakfast food into a shape conversation.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

A bagel is bread shaped like a ring: boiled for a minute, then baked, which gives it a shiny crust and a chewy middle. The hole is not decoration — it helps the thick dough cook all the way through.

What does it mean?

Name the breakfast food asks the child to pull one word from memory instead of pointing at it. Naming is a bigger jump than pointing: the answer has to come from inside.

What does the child need to know?

If bagel will not come out, accept circle, bread or donut-shaped and offer the word gently after — new words arrive on the third or fourth hearing, not the first.

Why this matters

Breakfast foods repeat every morning, which makes them the highest-value vocabulary in the house — one good week of breakfast words pays off for years.

What it teaches

Recall without pointing, the word circle, and morning routine language.

Words to learn

bagelholeringbreakfastchewycircle

Say this to your child

“Look — bread with a window! Round and round the edge... and through the hole! What is this called? A bagel. Can you say it? Ba-gel.”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and let a finger travel the outside edge — all the way around, no gaps. Then poke through the hole and say through. Give the child the finger-poke turn. Last, ask the child to name it: the word bagel, out loud, with whatever pronunciation arrives.

Look closer at the picture

Some children try to put a finger through the picture’s hole — let them. Touching the hole is the bagel’s most honest lesson.

Ask your child

What is this food? Where is the hole? What goes through the hole? Is it big or small?

What your child can say or do

Bagel! / Circle bread. / Hole! / My finger through.

Out in the real world

Bagels live at breakfast counters and bakery shelves — the child who knows the word gets to order by name, which is a very big feeling.

Try it together

Bagel I Spy: hide the card somewhere a circle peeks out — a plate rack, a jar lid — and hunt for the circle. Circles hide everywhere once you look.

Understanding check

Ask what is in the middle of a bagel. The answer is nothing, a hole, or a demonstrated finger — all three pass.

This lesson pairs with the Bagel flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Cafeteria.

CAFETERIA LESSON · CAFETERIA · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Banana — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches one — the seed of all counting — with the fruit a child can peel alone, and turns snack prep into finger practice.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

A banana is a long curved fruit with a peel that splits open in strips. It grows pointing upward in big bunches on plants that are actually giant herbs, not trees.

What does it mean?

Count one banana is a counting lesson hiding inside a snack order. Before children count to ten, they need the idea of one — exactly one — and the banana delivers it.

What does the child need to know?

Hold up one finger with the word one, every single time. The finger is the anchor: one banana, one finger, one child eating it.

Why this matters

Bananas come pre-wrapped, need no knife and travel anywhere, so the counting game can ride along to the park, the car seat and the stroller cup holder.

What it teaches

The number one as a real concept, pincer peel grip, and sequencing: peel, then eat.

Words to learn

bananaonepeelyellowcurvedopen

Say this to your child

“One banana — hold up one finger, like this. Can you pinch the top? Pull down... down... down. The banana opens! We had one banana. One!”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and hold up one finger together — one banana. Count a real banana if one is near: one. Then let the child pinch the stem tip and pull the peel down in strips, saying down each time. Eat the banana in bites and hold up one finger again at the end — all gone, there was one.

Look closer at the picture

Watch for the child offering the second finger — two! That is the next lesson arriving on its own, and it deserves a yes.

Ask your child

How many bananas? Where does the peel go? What color is the inside? What color is the outside?

What your child can say or do

One! / Nana! / Open it. / Down, down, down.

Out in the real world

Bananas ride in stroller bags and diaper packs everywhere — the counting game can start in the produce aisle, where the bunches hang in plain sight.

Try it together

Peel-and-pretend: after eating half, the empty peel becomes a boat, a phone or a smile — hold the curve to your mouth and let the child hear the new word.

Understanding check

Put two bananas on the table and ask for one. A child who takes exactly one — and maybe announces one — has the concept.

This lesson pairs with the Banana flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Cafeteria.

CAFETERIA LESSON · CAFETERIA · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Blueberries — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson uses the smallest food on the tray to teach the biggest early skill: one-to-one counting, one berry at a time.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Blueberries are small round berries, dark blue with a frosted look, that grow on bushes in clusters. They are soft enough for new eaters and sweet enough to keep the counting honest.

What does it mean?

Count the berries turns a snack into a math lesson. Each berry is one point of a finger, one number word, one swallow — the full counting loop in miniature.

What does the child need to know?

Count small: three to five berries is a real session at age two. The win is the rhythm — touch, say, eat — not the total.

Why this matters

Tiny countable food lets a child do the whole job alone: pick, count, eat, repeat. No help, no waiting, all momentum.

What it teaches

One-to-one counting, pincer grip, and the color blue in its only natural food.

Words to learn

blueberriesberrybluelittlecountmore

Say this to your child

“Let us count the berries — touch one, say one. One... two... three! Now eat one and count again. How many now? Two! You ate one!”

Step by step

  1. Pour a small pile on the tray and count them into a cup together, touching each one: one, two, three. Then reverse — eat one, count what is left. End by holding up the card and asking what color the berries are, then finding three blue things in the room.

Look closer at the picture

Watch whether the finger touches each berry once — skipping or double-touching is normal at two and smooths out with practice, not correction.

Ask your child

How many berries? What color are they? Where did the eaten one go? Can you find blue in this room?

What your child can say or do

Blue ones! / One, two! / More berries. / Little balls.

Out in the real world

Blueberries ride in little cups on real cafeteria trays — the card is rehearsing a sight the child will meet at every school lunch from now on.

Try it together

Berry hunt: hide five washable blue things — blocks, lids, crayons — around the rug and count them into a cup like a harvest. The counting is the game.

Understanding check

Line up three crackers and three blueberries. Ask which line has berries and count each aloud. Touch-counting three in a row passes the check.

This lesson pairs with the Blueberries flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Cafeteria.

CAFETERIA LESSON · CAFETERIA · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Bread — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the bread card through its many costumes — loaf, roll, slice — and plants the counting word one along the way.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Bread is flour and water made alive with yeast, then baked. The round loaf on the card has three slashes across the top — cuts a baker makes so the loaf can swell without tearing.

What does it mean?

Count one bread roll is the number one lesson arriving a second way. Repetition across different foods is how one stops being a word and becomes an idea.

What does the child need to know?

Bread words multiply fast — loaf, roll, bun, slice — so pick one per session. Today the roll; tomorrow the loaf; the slice can wait for sandwich week.

Why this matters

Bread shows up at every meal in every culture on Earth, which makes it the most useful food word any child will ever own.

What it teaches

The number one in a new costume, bakery vocabulary, and the kneading motion.

Words to learn

breadrollloafonebakeflour

Say this to your child

“Bread! One loaf — hold up one finger. One roll. Can you pat the dough? Pat, pat, pat — that is how bread gets ready for the oven.”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and find the three lines on top — stripes! Then count a real roll or slice: one. Let the child pat the air like kneading dough, pat-pat-pat, and finish by asking what bread turns into — toast, sandwich, crumbs — with any answer welcome.

Look closer at the picture

Watch for the child flattening the air-pat into a clap — clapping is close enough, and the motion will settle into patting with practice.

Ask your child

What is this food? How many rolls? What does bread turn into? Where does bread live — on the counter or in the fridge?

What your child can say or do

Bread! / One roll. / Toast! / Pat pat pat.

Out in the real world

Bakeries and bread aisles are everywhere — a walk past the bakery case becomes a live bread lesson, warm smells included.

Try it together

Baker, baker: the child kneads pretend dough, pats it round, scores three lines in the air with a finger, and slides it into the pretend oven — then serves the loaf to the room.

Understanding check

Show the bread card beside any other card and ask how many bread rolls are on the table. One — with a finger held up — passes.

This lesson pairs with the Bread flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Cafeteria.

CAFETERIA LESSON · CAFETERIA · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Broccoli — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches broccoli the way children already see it — as little trees — and uses matching to train careful looking.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Broccoli is a green vegetable grown for its flower buds, eaten before they open. The thick stalk holds up a crown of bumpy florets that look exactly like a tiny tree.

What does it mean?

Match the broccoli asks the child to find two of the same — same shape, same color, same tree. Matching is the toddler version of sorting, and sorting is the root of math.

What does the child need to know?

The tree story is not a trick; it is a handle. Children who call broccoli a tree eat more of it, and the botany catches up later — the florets really are buds.

Why this matters

Green vegetables are the shelf’s hardest sell and its biggest prize; giving the child a game instead of a lecture changes the whole negotiation.

What it teaches

Same-and-different spotting, the word tree as a shape handle, and brave-bite courage.

Words to learn

broccolitreegreenmatchfloretcrunchy

Say this to your child

“Broccoli! A little tree on a trunk. Make your hand be a tree — fingers up! Now find the matching tree... under which cup? Lift it slow... there it is!”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and trace the tree with a finger — trunk, then bumpy leaves. Ask the child to hold up a hand-tree: fingers up, arm the trunk. Then hide a second broccoli card or picture under a cup and play match-the-tree until the crown is found. Any real broccoli at the table earns one brave bite, dips allowed.

Look closer at the picture

Watch the matching, not the eating. A child who matches perfectly but skips the bite is winning the lesson; the bites follow on their own schedule.

Ask your child

What does broccoli look like? Where is the trunk? Can you find the matching tree? What color is the tree?

What your child can say or do

Tree! / Little trees. / Match it! / Green one.

Out in the real world

Broccoli rides every salad bar and kids’ menu — the tree handle travels to restaurants, grandma’s table and the freezer aisle without any re-teaching.

Try it together

Forest walk: line up five vegetable cards like trees and let a toy animal walk the forest, stopping to sniff each tree — the broccoli tree gets the longest sniff.

Understanding check

Mix the broccoli card into three other food cards and ask the child to find the tree. One correct grab — tree declared or not — passes.

This lesson pairs with the Broccoli flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Cafeteria.

CAFETERIA LESSON · CAFETERIA · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Burrito — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the burrito as a mystery package — a food sleeping bag with a surprise inside — and turns finding it into a vocabulary hunt.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

A burrito is a soft flour tortilla wrapped around beans, rice and vegetables, with the ends folded in so nothing escapes. It is a whole meal that fits in two hands.

What does it mean?

Find the burrito asks the child to spot one named food hiding in a lineup — a search-and-name drill that is the engine of every look-and-find book they will ever love.

What does the child need to know?

Roll a towel around a toy and you have a demo burrito: the wrap IS the lesson. Foods that hide inside other things are endlessly funny at this age.

Why this matters

Burritos are the child’s first lesson that food can be a package — and wrapped foods travel to every picnic and car ride after this.

What it teaches

Search-and-name focus, the words roll and wrap, and pretend-play plotting.

Words to learn

burritorollwrapinsidebeanstortilla

Say this to your child

“A burrito is a food sleeping bag — everything rolled up inside! What is hiding in ours? Let us unwrap it... beans! Rice! Now wrap it back up, tight tight tight.”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and ask what is inside — lift the flap of your imagination and name the beans and rice. Then wrap a toy in a small blanket, roll it burrito-tight and ask what the blanket food is called. Unwrap it together, then rewrap. Finish with the card: find the burrito among two other cards.

Look closer at the picture

Watch whether the child checks the open end of the card’s burrito — peeking into the filling is exactly the curiosity the card is built to start.

Ask your child

What is a burrito? What is inside? Where do the ends go? Can you roll it back up?

What your child can say or do

Burrito! / Rolled up. / Beans inside. / Open it!

Out in the real world

Burrito lines exist at every food court and family table — the child who knows the wrap story watches real ones being rolled like theater.

Try it together

Burrito roll-up: the child lies at the end of a blanket, grips the edges and rolls — gently — into a human burrito. What is inside? A silly, wrapped-up kid.

Understanding check

Ask what a burrito is made of. Any inside-answer — beans, rice, blanket, tortilla — passes the check.

This lesson pairs with the Burrito flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Cafeteria.

CAFETERIA LESSON · CAFETERIA · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Cafeteria Tray — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the one card that is not food — the tray — and uses its compartments to run the room’s best sorting game.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

A cafeteria tray is a flat board with five compartments and a round plate in the middle. Every food gets its own spot, which keeps the soup out of the pudding and the peas off the cookie.

What does it mean?

Match the tray asks the child to find the same layout — five boxes and a circle. Matching a pattern, not just a picture, is a step up in looking carefully.

What does the child need to know?

The tray is the whole room in one object: it is where short-order sorting happens at every real lunch. The card rehearses that map before the real tray arrives.

Why this matters

Compartment thinking — one thing per box — is how young children learn categories, and the tray is the friendliest grid they will ever meet.

What it teaches

Pattern matching, one-to-one sorting, and the spatial words in, on and beside.

Words to learn

traycompartmentsspotsplatematchsort

Say this to your child

“This is the tray — every food has its own spot! Count the boxes: one, two, three, four, five — and a round plate! Where do we park the milk? Right there. And the fruit? Its own box!”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and count the compartments out loud — one, two, three, four, five — then find the round plate. Ask the child to point to each spot as it is named. Then play match-the-tray with two or more cards mixed in. For the long version, draw a big paper tray with five boxes and let the child park one snack in each box.

Look closer at the picture

Watch for the child lining toys up in rows after this lesson — compartment thinking leaks into play, and that leak is the lesson working.

Ask your child

How many spots does the tray have? Where is the round plate? Which spot would the apple go in? Can you match the tray?

What your child can say or do

Tray! / Five boxes. / My spot. / Milk goes here.

Out in the real world

School lunches everywhere arrive on a divided tray — the child who knows the map walks into the cafeteria line already fluent.

Try it together

Paper tray lunch: draw five boxes on paper, deal five food cards, and let the child deal one card per box — main dish here, fruit there, drink last. Deal again tomorrow.

Understanding check

Draw a quick tray with five boxes and ask which box the drink goes in. Any pointed or stated spot — box or plate — passes.

This lesson pairs with the Cafeteria Tray flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Cafeteria.

CAFETERIA LESSON · CAFETERIA · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Carrots — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches counting to three with the crunchiest vegetable on the tray — and the rabbit story that makes every crunch louder.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

A carrot is an orange root vegetable that grows underground, pointy end down, leafy top up. It is sweet for a vegetable, which is why it is usually the first one children accept.

What does it mean?

Count the carrots is a three-count with a built-in reward: each counted carrot can be a crunched carrot. Counting with sound — snap, snap, snap — sticks better than counting in silence.

What does the child need to know?

Three is the target, not ten. A child who counts one-two-three and eats three carrots has completed a full math-and-snack cycle; extension can wait for tomorrow.

Why this matters

Carrots ride in every lunchbox and every soup — the word and the count rehearse together for years after this lesson.

What it teaches

Counting to three, loud chewing confidence, and the color orange.

Words to learn

carrotsthreeorangecrunchrabbittop

Say this to your child

“Count with me — one... two... three carrots! Rabbits eat carrots — can you crunch like a rabbit? Nibble nibble! Now hop! One hop for each carrot — hop, hop, hop!”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and count the carrots slowly — one, two, three — touching each one. Make the rabbit connection: carrots are what rabbits crunch. Then line up three real carrot rounds and count them onto the plate, eating one per number. Finish by hopping once for each carrot — three hops, three carrots, one proud rabbit.

Look closer at the picture

Watch whether the count and the touch stay together — if the finger races ahead of the words, slow the whole game down and count at finger speed.

Ask your child

How many carrots? What color are they? Who loves to eat carrots? Can you crunch like a bunny?

What your child can say or do

Three! / Orange ones. / Hop hop! / Crunch crunch.

Out in the real world

Carrots arrive whole at every salad bar and in every veggie cup — the count-three habit can ride in the lunchbox every day.

Try it together

Feed the rabbit: cut a bunny face from paper, tape it to a cup, and feed the rabbit one carrot at a time — counting each hop of the carrot into the cup. Three carrots later, the rabbit is full and so is the counter.

Understanding check

Line up four carrots or carrot cards and ask the child to give you three. Handing over exactly three — counted or grabbed — passes.

This lesson pairs with the Carrots flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Cafeteria.

CAFETERIA LESSON · CAFETERIA · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Celery — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the number two with the vegetable that makes the most noise — and turns celery into a buildable snack project.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Celery grows in tall, ribbed stalks bundled together at the base. It is mostly water, which is why it snaps cleanly, crunches loudly and tastes like cool nothing — a perfect carrier for fills and dips.

What does it mean?

Count the celery sticks is the two-count: one, two. After one and three, two is the middle number children master — and sticks are the clearest two-things picture there is.

What does the child need to know?

The crunch is the lesson. A vegetable a child can hear themselves eat gets eaten again; quiet vegetables need fillings and fanfare.

Why this matters

Celery is the base of ants on a log, the classic build-your-own snack — this lesson rehearses the build before the real one.

What it teaches

Counting two, the fill-and-press motion, and listening for crunch as a food skill.

Words to learn

celerystickstwocrunchribsfill

Say this to your child

“Two sticks! Count them: one, two. Two celery sticks. Listen when we crunch... CRUNCH! Can you hear it? Now let us fill the groove — cheese in the boat, three little ants on top. One, two, three!”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and count the sticks — one, two — then cross two fingers in the air the same way. Snap a raw bean or a crisp cracker near your ear and talk about the sound celery makes. Fill a real celery groove with cream cheese, press three raisins in, and count them: three ants riding two sticks.

Look closer at the picture

Watch the filling finger: pushing spread into a groove takes more wrist control than spreading on flat bread, and wobbles are the exercise.

Ask your child

How many sticks? What sound does celery make? What did we put in the groove? How many ants?

What your child can say or do

Two sticks! / Crunch! / Ants on a log. / More cheese.

Out in the real world

Celery arrives on every veggie platter and in every soup base — the two-stick count and the crunch game ride along to every party tray.

Try it together

Celery orchestra: fill three celery sticks three ways — plain, cream cheese, peanut butter — and take a loud bite of each. Which crunch is biggest? Award the gold medal.

Understanding check

Hold up the celery card and ask how many sticks. Two — said, shown on fingers, or counted aloud — passes.

This lesson pairs with the Celery flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Cafeteria.

CAFETERIA LESSON · CAFETERIA · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Cereal — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the cereal card as the morning routine’s star — named out loud, stirred in circles, and counted ring by ring.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Breakfast cereal is grain cooked, shaped and toasted — into flakes, puffs or the rings on this card — and eaten with cold milk from a big bowl.

What does it mean?

Name the cereal asks for a word from memory again, but from a noisy field: breakfast shelves are crowded, and picking one word from many is the real workout.

What does the child need to know?

Cereal names are brands and shapes mixed together in a child’s head; any breakfast word that shows up — cereal, rings, bowl — is a correct answer today.

Why this matters

Cereal is often the first food a child pours, spoons and serves solo, so this card quietly rehearses a whole independence routine.

What it teaches

Recall in a crowded field, wrist rotation for stirring, and finger counting with rings.

Words to learn

cerealbowlringsmilkstirbreakfast

Say this to your child

“Cereal! Rings in a big bowl. Let us pour — glug glug! Stir one slow circle... now fast! Look — rings on my fingers! Count my hats: one, two, three...”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and name it together, then hunt the room for a bowl — any bowl — and set it beside the card. Mime the pour: glug, glug. Mime the stir: one slow circle. If real ring cereal is nearby, press one ring on each fingertip and count the ten little hats before eating them off, one by one.

Look closer at the picture

Watch the stir direction: whichever way the child stirs is fine and usually sticks for life. Counterclockwise stirrers exist and they are magnificent.

Ask your child

What food is this? Where does it go — in a bowl or a cup? What do we pour on top? How many rings on your fingers?

What your child can say or do

Cereal! / Rings! / Pour milk. / Hat on my finger.

Out in the real world

Cereal boxes live at child eye level in every store — the naming game works in the aisle, where the boxes are the flashcards.

Try it together

Cereal shop: prop up three breakfast cards as a menu, hand over pretend money and take an order — one cereal, please! Serving the order is the whole game.

Understanding check

Ask what we eat cereal from. The answer bowl — pointed at, fetched, or mimed with two hands — passes.

This lesson pairs with the Cereal flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Cafeteria.

CAFETERIA LESSON · CAFETERIA · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Cheese — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the cheese card through its square shape — matched on the card, stacked on the plate, and traced back to the milk it came from.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Cheese is milk that has been thickened with a special culture and pressed into shape. The card shows one yellow slice angled like a diamond — the everyday sandwich cheese.

What does it mean?

Match the cheese is the matching drill again, but the cheese square has a trick: turned one way it is a square, turned another it is a diamond. Same cheese, two names.

What does the child need to know?

Keep the geometry light — square is the word of the day, diamond is the bonus when the slice sits on its corner. Do not grade the turn.

Why this matters

Cheese is the protein most picky eaters accept first, which makes this card a reliable win and a gateway to the whole dairy shelf.

What it teaches

Shape words, stacking balance, and the milk-to-cheese origin story.

Words to learn

cheesesquareyellowslicestackmilk

Say this to your child

“A cheese square! Trace the edges — four sides. Turn it... it is still cheese! Let us stack: one, two, three squares high. And here is the secret — cheese is milk that learned to hold still.”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and trace the square’s four edges — one, two, three, four sides. Turn the card a quarter turn: still cheese! Then stack real cheese squares two high, then three, admiring the tower before eating it down to one. Finish with the story: cheese is milk you can hold.

Look closer at the picture

Watch the stacking hand: centering one square on another is real balance work, and topples are part of the physics lesson.

Ask your child

What shape is the cheese? How many edges? What food does cheese come from? Can you stack two?

What your child can say or do

Square! / Cheese stack! / From milk. / Fell down!

Out in the real world

Cheese squares ride in every lunchbox beside crackers and fruit — the stacking game works anywhere a slice can lie flat.

Try it together

Cracker cafe: three crackers, three cheese squares, one customer — build three open-face sandwiches and serve them with a flourish. The chef eats the leftovers.

Understanding check

Show the cheese card and ask what shape it is. Square, diamond, or four sides traced with a finger — all pass.

This lesson pairs with the Cheese flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Cafeteria.

CAFETERIA LESSON · CAFETERIA · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Chicken Nuggets — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson uses the deck’s friendliest finger food to run a five-count — with dip cups as the reward stations.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Chicken nuggets are small pieces of chicken wrapped in seasoned breading and baked or fried until golden. They are sized for two bites, which is exactly a five-year-old’s mouth math.

What does it mean?

Count the nuggets is the count-to-five milestone. Five is the biggest number most two-year-olds track with one-to-one touching, and five is how many nuggets the card shows.

What does the child need to know?

Let the count be slow and the dips be three. A child who touches each nugget while saying the numbers is doing real math even if the order wobbles.

Why this matters

Nuggets are often the first protein a cautious eater accepts, which makes this the highest-leverage counting plate in the building.

What it teaches

Counting to five with touch, dip-and-bite sequencing, and comparing more or less.

Words to learn

nuggetsfivegoldendipcrunchmore

Say this to your child

“Five on the plate — count them: one, two, three, four, five! Two dip cups — which one first? Nugget one goes... plop! Nugget two... Now wait — how many are left? Three! You ate two!”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and count the nuggets together — one through five, touching each. Set out two dip cups and count the stations. Then eat by the numbers: nugget one in dip one, nugget two in dip two, and so on. Pause after three and ask how many are left — the subtraction question arrives on its own.

Look closer at the picture

Watch for one-to-one touching. If the finger skips, hold the plate still and count at finger speed — speed is the enemy of an honest count.

Ask your child

How many nuggets? How many did you eat? How many are left? Which dip is winning?

What your child can say or do

Five! / Two left! / Dip dip! / This one wins.

Out in the real world

Nuggets ride every kids’ menu on Earth — the count-five habit turns a restaurant order into a live math plate.

Try it together

Dip taste-off: three dips, five nuggets, one judge. Rate each dip with a thumbs up, sideways or down, and keep a running total of the winner. Democracy, but crunchy.

Understanding check

Cover the plate after the meal and ask how many nuggets there were. Five — recalled, counted on fingers, or shown — passes.

This lesson pairs with the Chicken Nuggets flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Cafeteria.

CAFETERIA LESSON · CAFETERIA · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Chicken — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the drumstick as the food with a built-in handle — matched picture-to-plate and held just like the card shows.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

A chicken drumstick is the lower part of a chicken’s leg, roasted until the skin turns golden and crinkled. The bone at the end is the handle that made it famous.

What does it mean?

Match the chicken asks the child to connect the card to the real plate — the picture-to-object leap that makes every food card in this room work.

What does the child need to know?

Hold the match honestly: card beside plate, shapes compared out loud — same shape, same color, same handle. The comparison is the lesson; the bite is optional and usually follows.

Why this matters

Drumsticks come with their own grip, so this card teaches holding before eating — the rare food that trains the hand without a utensil.

What it teaches

Picture-to-object matching, grip strength, and gentle animal-to-food storytelling.

Words to learn

chickendrumstickhandleboneroastgolden

Say this to your child

“Same shape, same color — it is the chicken from the card! Hold it by the little bone... can you wave? Hello, drumstick! Listen — hear the crunch when we bite?”

Step by step

  1. Show the card, then bring the plate and lay the drumstick beside it. Compare out loud: shape, color, handle. Let the child hold the real one by the bone and wave hello. Eat a bite and listen for the crunch — skin is the loud part. Finish by asking where drumsticks come from, and follow the child’s lead with the honest short version.

Look closer at the picture

Some children go quiet at the animal story. Keep it simple and kind: chickens are animals, and drumstick is what we call this part of the dinner — no lecture needed either way.

Ask your child

What food is this? Where do we hold it? What part is the handle? Does yours match the card?

What your child can say or do

Drumstick! / Hold the bone. / Same one! / Crunchy skin.

Out in the real world

Drumsticks arrive at picnics, family tables and every holiday plate — the handle-hold travels everywhere dinner is served.

Try it together

Drumstick band: tap two breadsticks or carrot sticks like drumsticks on the table edge — one loud tap, one soft tap — then take a real drumstick bite as the encore.

Understanding check

Show the card and ask where we hold a drumstick. A point to the narrow end, a grab at the real bone, or the word handle passes.

This lesson pairs with the Chicken flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Cafeteria.

CAFETERIA LESSON · CAFETERIA · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Chocolate Milk — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the tray’s most recognizable carton — named from across the room — and runs a gentle compare with its white cousin.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Chocolate milk is milk mixed with cocoa and a little sugar, served in a small carton with the words printed on the front. It is the same white milk inside a brown costume.

What does it mean?

Name the drink asks for recall at a distance — the carton is recognizable across a whole cafeteria, which makes it the ideal first far-name game.

What does the child need to know?

Pair the two milk cards side by side and let the child tell them apart by color first, name second. The comparison does the teaching; the labels just confirm it.

Why this matters

Drinks are named before foods at this age — cartons are held daily, and a child who can name the drink can request it, which is real power.

What it teaches

Distance naming, color-based sorting, and same-but-different comparison.

Words to learn

chocolate milkmilkbrownwhitecartonsip

Say this to your child

“Two milk cartons! This one is brown — chocolate milk. This one is white — regular milk. Run and get the chocolate one! ... Now look: same box, different color. Sip and guess — which cup is which?”

Step by step

  1. Set the chocolate-milk card at one end of the table and the white milk card at the other. Name each one, then ask for them from across the room — run and fetch! Once fetched, compare the cartons: same shape, different colors. Pour a splash of each into clear cups and guess before tasting which is which.

Look closer at the picture

Watch the fetch: a child who runs to the correct card from across the room has done distance naming — the far end of the naming skill range.

Ask your child

Which one is chocolate milk? What color is each carton? Are the boxes the same shape? Which do you want today?

What your child can say or do

Choc milk! / Brown one! / Same box. / This one!

Out in the real world

School cafeterias hand out both milk cartons side by side every day — this lesson is rehearsal for a choice the child will make a thousand times.

Try it together

Milk mail: hide both cards in different rooms, then deliver letters — take the brown letter to the kitchen! Take the white one to the sofa! Fetching by name is the game.

Understanding check

Mix the two milk cards with a juice card and ask for chocolate milk. One correct grab, from any distance, passes.

This lesson pairs with the Chocolate Milk flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Cafeteria.

CAFETERIA LESSON · CAFETERIA · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Cookie — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson turns the cookie card into a counting picture — the chocolate spots are the counters — and gives small hands the best baking job there is.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

A cookie is a small flat cake baked until firm, and this one is studded with chocolate chips. The card shows the wavy edge and scattered spots — every chip a counting target.

What does it mean?

Match the cookie hides a count inside a match: two cookies side by side are only the same if they have the same spots. Looking that closely is pattern reading.

What does the child need to know?

Count three to five chips, not the whole cookie. The spots are irregular on purpose — counting scattered things is harder than counting rows, and that is the point.

Why this matters

Cookies are the food children negotiate for hardest, so attaching a counting job to one is the oldest trade in the parenting playbook — and it works.

What it teaches

Counting scattered objects, spot-to-spot matching, and press-down finger strength.

Words to learn

cookiechipsspotsroundmatchbake

Say this to your child

“Round cookie, wavy edge — and look, chocolate spots! Count them: one... two... three... can you find more? Now — does this cookie match that cookie? Same round? Same spots?”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and count the spots slowly — one, two, three — then ask if the child can find more. Show a second treat card and ask whether the cookies match: same shape, same round, different spots. If baking is an option, give the child five chips to press into each round of dough — five pushes, one cookie, zero complaints.

Look closer at the picture

Watch for spot-touching with one finger — the pincer poke is the count’s honest form, and it is fine if the finger revisits the same spot twice.

Ask your child

How many spots? Do the two cookies match? What shape is the cookie? What do we press into the dough?

What your child can say or do

Spots! / One, two, three. / Not same! / My turn to press.

Out in the real world

Cookies live in bakery cases and lunchboxes everywhere — the spot-count works on any cookie anywhere, which makes this lesson portable for life.

Try it together

Cookie factory: roll play dough into rounds, press buttons or beads in as chips, count each cookie’s spots, and deliver orders to the room. Factory chaos is the fun part.

Understanding check

Ask what is on top of the cookie. Chips, spots, chocolate, or a demonstrated poke at the picture — all pass.

This lesson pairs with the Cookie flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Cafeteria.

CAFETERIA LESSON · CAFETERIA · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Corn — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the corn cob as a pattern machine — rows to trace, rows to eat — and sends the child on a yellow hunt.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Corn grows as a cob: hundreds of yellow kernels in straight rows around a woody center, wrapped in green husks. Each kernel is a seed — the whole cob is a seed packet.

What does it mean?

Name the corn is a recall drill again, but the cob adds a bonus: its rows make it the tray’s best pattern object, and patterns are where math begins.

What does the child need to know?

Trace the rows before eating them. A finger running down a kernel row is a pre-writing stroke — a straight line with bumps — and the child will trace it over and over.

Why this matters

Corn arrives on the cob at picnics and cut in cups at school; either way the yellow rows are unmistakable, so this word pays off in both costumes.

What it teaches

Pattern tracing, row-by-row eating strategy, and the color yellow.

Words to learn

corncobrowskernelsyellowhusk

Say this to your child

“Look at the corn — rows and rows of little yellow kernels! Run your finger down... tick tick tick. Now another row! Can you find three yellow things in this room? Hunt!”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and run a finger down one row — tick, tick, tick — then another row beside it. Talk about the pattern: rows going up, rows going across. If a real cob is near, eat it row by row like mowing a tiny lawn. Finish with a yellow hunt: three yellow things in the room, corn card held up as the trophy.

Look closer at the picture

Watch the tracing finger: it should travel the row, not hop kernel to kernel. A smooth slide is the pre-writing win; hopping is tomorrow’s refinement.

Ask your child

What food is this? What color are the kernels? Can your finger ride a row? What else is yellow?

What your child can say or do

Corn! / Bumpy! / Yellow one. / Tick tick tick.

Out in the real world

Corn on the cob is a summer picnic fixture and a popcorn factory all in one — the row game works on both the dinner cob and the popping kind.

Try it together

Corn mowing: with a real cob or a drawn one, mow the kernels row by row with a finger — beep beep, here comes the mower — then eat a real row the same way.

Understanding check

Ask what covers a corn cob. Kernels, seeds, yellow bumps, or a traced row — all pass.

This lesson pairs with the Corn flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Cafeteria.

CAFETERIA LESSON · CAFETERIA · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Crackers — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the count to three with the shelf’s flattest food — and answers the question every curious child asks: why the dots?

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Crackers are thin baked squares, docked with tiny holes so they bake flat and crisp. The card shows three saltines stacked like tiles — the count built right into the picture.

What does it mean?

Count the crackers is the three-count in its flattest form: three squares, clearly separate, impossible to miscount. It is the confidence builder between two and five.

What does the child need to know?

The snap is the hook. Crackers break cleanly in half with a satisfying click — a food that doubles as a percussion section keeps its audience.

Why this matters

Crackers are the carrying case of snack food — cheese rides on them, soup dunk them, and the three-count rehearses on every tray.

What it teaches

Counting three, snap strength, and topping-and-serving pretend play.

Words to learn

crackersthreesquaresnapcrispholes

Say this to your child

“Count them — one, two, three crackers! See the tiny dots? Little holes so they bake flat and crispy. Listen — snap! One cracker, two pieces. Now we build: cheese here, banana there... order up!”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and count the crackers — one, two, three — touching each square. Point out the little dots: holes that let the cracker stay flat. Snap a real cracker in half, listen to the click, and count the pieces — one cracker became two! Then build three open-face crackers with toppings and serve them like a café.

Look closer at the picture

Watch the snap grip: thumbs on top, fingers under, one clean bend. The successful first snap gets repeated about forty times — budget crackers accordingly.

Ask your child

How many crackers? What are the little dots? What did the snap sound like? What did we put on top?

What your child can say or do

Three! / Snap! / Dots. / Order up!

Out in the real world

Cracker packets ride in every diaper bag — the three-count works at restaurants before the meal arrives, which is exactly when a counting game earns its keep.

Try it together

Cracker café: three crackers, three toppings, one stuffed animal customer. Take the order, build the plates, deliver with a bow. Tips accepted in pretend coins.

Understanding check

Ask how many crackers the card shows. Three — said, counted aloud, or tapped — passes.

This lesson pairs with the Crackers flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Cafeteria.

CAFETERIA LESSON · CAFETERIA · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Cucumber — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the cucumber through its superpower — coolness — and gives the mildest vegetable in the room its full moment.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

A cucumber is a long green fruit (yes, fruit) with dark skin and pale, watery flesh. It is 95 percent water, which is why slices feel cool and taste like a crisp drink.

What does it mean?

Name the vegetable is the category game: of all the tray’s foods, which one is a vegetable? Naming a category member trains sorting without saying so.

What does the child need to know?

The eye trick is the hook: a cool cucumber slice on each closed eye is ten seconds of spa magic, and a food that becomes a game piece gets a second chance at lunch.

Why this matters

Cucumber is the mildest crunch there is — the vegetable cautious eaters accept first, which makes this the gateway card for the whole green shelf.

What it teaches

Category naming, temperature words, and gentle self-serve confidence.

Words to learn

cucumbercoolgreenslicecrispvegetable

Say this to your child

“Cucumber! The cool green one. Hold a slice on each eye... ten seconds... brrr, cool! Now a nibble — hear the little crunch? Which other cards are vegetables? Let us sort them out.”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and name the vegetable together. Trace the whole cucumber, then the round slices fanned beside it. Hand the child a real slice to hold on each closed eye — ten cool seconds — then invite a nibble. Finish by asking which other cards show vegetables, and sort two or three together.

Look closer at the picture

Watch the eye-hold: some children peek immediately, some hold it forever. Either way the temperature memory sticks — cool belongs to cucumber now.

Ask your child

What vegetable is this? How does the slice feel? What other cards are vegetables? Is it crunchy or soft?

What your child can say or do

Cool! / Green one. / On my eyes! / Crunchy a little.

Out in the real world

Cucumber rides in every salad and every water pitcher at restaurants — the coolness story explains both, and the child now owns the word for it.

Try it together

Veggie sort: mix three food cards with three vegetable cards and deal them into two piles — vegetables here, everything else there. Sort again by color for round two.

Understanding check

Ask what the cucumber feels like. Cool, cold, wet, or a demonstrated shiver — all pass.

This lesson pairs with the Cucumber flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Cafeteria.

CAFETERIA LESSON · CAFETERIA · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Egg — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the egg as the tray’s simplest shape — one smooth oval — and turns peeling a real one into the finest finger workout in the kitchen.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

An egg is a smooth oval laid by a hen, with a thin shell, a white and a golden yolk inside. Boiled for ten minutes, it becomes a peeled-and-eaten classic.

What does it mean?

Match the egg trains shape eyes: the oval is a stretched circle, and spotting it among the tray’s rounds and squares is a real geometry start.

What does the child need to know?

Peeling is the gift of this card. Cracking the shell, rolling the egg, picking off bits in slow pieces — no kitchen job rewards patience more clearly.

Why this matters

Eggs show up at every breakfast table on Earth, and the oval shows up in every shape lesson after — this card feeds both pipelines.

What it teaches

Oval recognition, crack-peel fine motor work, and cupped-hands care.

Words to learn

eggovalshellpeelsmoothnest

Say this to your child

“An egg — a circle that stretched into an oval! Make a nest with your hands... now lay the egg inside, gentle. Ready to peel a real one? Tap, tap... roll it... pick the shell — bit by bit. There is breakfast!”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and trace the oval with one finger — a circle that stretched. Cup both hands into a nest and let the child lay the card inside like an egg in a nest. Then boil, cool and crack a real egg together: tap, roll under a palm, pick the shell off bit by bit. Eat the reveal.

Look closer at the picture

Watch the peeling fingers: small shell bits are the exercise, and the child who picks for two full minutes is doing better fine-motor work than any worksheet.

Ask your child

What shape is an egg? Where does an egg sleep — in a nest or a basket? What color is the shell? What was hiding inside?

What your child can say or do

Oval! / In my nest. / Peel it! / Cracked it!

Out in the real world

Eggs wait in nearly every refrigerator on Earth — the peel job rehearses any morning, and the nest story rides along to any park with birds.

Try it together

Nest delivery: hide three egg cards around the room, hand the child a paper-bag nest, and send them collecting — one egg per trip, carried gently, counted at the end.

Understanding check

Ask what shape an egg is. Oval, stretched circle, or an oval traced in the air — all pass.

This lesson pairs with the Egg flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Cafeteria.

CAFETERIA LESSON · CAFETERIA · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Fish — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the fish fillet as the sea’s gentlest food — matched to the card, flaked with a fork, and introduced with the sound every child already knows.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

A fish fillet is a boneless piece of fish, white and flaky inside, with light seasoning on top. It is the sea food most often served to small children because it is mild and soft.

What does it mean?

Match the fish runs the picture-to-plate drill again — and the fillet is the subtlest match on the shelf, since cooked fish looks less like swimming fish than any other card.

What does the child need to know?

Keep the sea story light and joyful: fish swim, fish on plates are food, and both can be true without a single awkward question. Follow the child’s lead.

Why this matters

Fish is the protein picky eaters side-eye first — arriving with a game, a fork and a sound effect lowers the stakes for everyone.

What it teaches

Picture-to-plate matching, fork flaking, and open-ended food courage.

Words to learn

fishfilletflakeforksoftglub

Say this to your child

“Fish! In the water it goes glub glub — on the plate it goes flake flake. Watch the fork lift the layers... like pages of a book! Your turn — make a fish boat on a cracker.”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and make the sound together — glub glub — then match the plate to the picture, side by side. Flake a corner with a fork, lifting the layers apart like pages. Let the child flake one piece and press it onto a cracker — a tiny fish boat. One brave bite caps it, dips allowed.

Look closer at the picture

Watch the fork grip: flaking needs a push-and-lift motion most two-year-olds get on the third try, and the third try is always the proudest.

Ask your child

What food is this? Where do fish live? What does the fork do to the fish? What did we build on the cracker?

What your child can say or do

Glub glub! / Flake it. / Fish boat! / Soft one.

Out in the real world

Fish lives on every restaurant menu as sticks, fillets and sandwiches — the flake-and-boat move works anywhere a fork and a cracker meet.

Try it together

Fishing pond: cut paper fish, clip a magnet to a string, and fish them out of a blue towel pond — each catch gets named and counted. Real fish crackers are the catch of the day.

Understanding check

Show the card and ask where fish live before dinner. Water, sea, or a glub-glub mime — all pass.

This lesson pairs with the Fish flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Cafeteria.

CAFETERIA LESSON · CAFETERIA · AGES 2–5 YEARS

French Fries — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson turns the tray’s most famous silhouette into a subtraction game — count the fries, eat one, count again.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

French fries are potatoes cut into sticks and fried or baked until golden. The card shows a white carton with fries standing at different heights — a little city skyline of potato.

What does it mean?

Count the fries and then count again after one disappears: that is subtraction in its tastiest form. The count that shrinks teaches more-than and less-than without any worksheet.

What does the child need to know?

Stand the fries upright for the count — a fry skyline counts better than a fry pile, and the different heights are part of the fun.

Why this matters

Fries are the food every child meets at every restaurant — attaching honest counting to them costs nothing and pays out all childhood.

What it teaches

Counting, take-away subtraction, and more-or-less comparison.

Words to learn

friescounttowerlessgonegolden

Say this to your child

“Stand them up — a fry city! Count the towers: one, two, three... Now eat one — crunch! How many now? Fewer! Again! One more gone... how many? The city shrinks!”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and count the standing fries — whatever number the picture gives. Then line up real fries like towers and count them. Eat one — loudly — and recount: how many now? Repeat until the skyline is gone, announcing the shrinking number each round. End by asking which had more: the first line or the last.

Look closer at the picture

Watch the recount: after eating, does the child recount from one or just announce the new number? Both are correct steps; recounting is the scaffolding, announcing is the growth.

Ask your child

How many fries now? Were there more before or after? Which is the tallest tower? What food are fries made from?

What your child can say or do

One less! / Three now. / More before! / Potato sticks!

Out in the real world

Fries arrive beside every restaurant kids’ meal — the disappearing count is the perfect pre-dinner game, played with the food itself.

Try it together

Fry skyline: build towers from standing fries on the plate, count each tower’s floors, then demolish city by city — one bite per floor. Demolish, count, repeat.

Understanding check

Line up three fries, eat one out of sight, and ask how many are left. Two — counted or announced — passes.

This lesson pairs with the French Fries flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Cafeteria.

CAFETERIA LESSON · CAFETERIA · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Fruit Salad — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the fruit salad as a color hunt — five fruits, five colors, one bowl — and gives the child the easiest kitchen job there is: the stir.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Fruit salad is many fruits cut small and tossed together — strawberries, kiwi, grapes, melon, pineapple — so every spoonful is a different mix. One bowl, many fruits.

What does it mean?

Find the fruit salad is a search among lookalikes — cups and bowls crowd the shelf, and the rainbow bowl is the stand-out. Spotting one among many is the daily work of every look-and-find page.

What does the child need to know?

Name a color per fruit as you go — red strawberry, green kiwi, purple grape. The bowl becomes a color review disguised as lunch.

Why this matters

Fruit salad rehearses the biggest idea on the shelf: many things can be one thing — many fruits, one salad. That idea is the seed of every group and set a child will ever sort.

What it teaches

Color naming, many-in-one thinking, and the big-spoon stir.

Words to learn

fruit saladbowlcolorsmixmanystir

Say this to your child

“A whole rainbow in one bowl! Red strawberry... green kiwi... purple grape — how many fruits? Many! Let us make ours: strawberries in, one stir. Kiwi in, one stir... Now guess the spoonful!”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and hunt the bowl’s colors — point and name each fruit. Ask how many fruits are hiding in there: many! Then build a real version: three soft fruits, one big spoon, one stir per fruit as it is named. Serve the mix and take turns guessing which fruit the next spoonful holds.

Look closer at the picture

Watch the guess: predicting the next spoonful is early probability — sometimes right, sometimes surprised, always delighted.

Ask your child

What colors live in the bowl? How many fruits is that? What did we stir in first? Which fruit will the next spoonful be?

What your child can say or do

Rainbow bowl! / Many fruits! / My stir. / I guess grape!

Out in the real world

Fruit cups and salad bars serve this exact bowl everywhere — the color hunt works on any fruit plate, any buffet, any summer table.

Try it together

Rainbow picnic: deal five fruit cards face up and go color hunting around the room for matching things — one toy per fruit color, parked beside its card. The card bowl fills with a toy rainbow.

Understanding check

Ask what fruit salad is. Many fruits, a mix, or a named trio of fruits — all pass.

This lesson pairs with the Fruit Salad flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Cafeteria.

Granola Bar — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the granola bar as the tray’s traveler — found in a lineup, broken on its lines, and counted piece by piece.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

A granola bar is oats and honey pressed into a rectangle and baked until it holds together. It travels in pockets and lunchboxes without crumbling — a picnic that fits in a palm.

What does it mean?

Find the granola bar is the search drill again — and the bar is the deck’s best camouflage exercise, since it is the only long brown rectangle among rounds and cups.

What does the child need to know?

Granola bars break along scored lines — press, snap, and the bar becomes two or three equal pieces. That snap is a fraction lesson wearing a wrapper.

Why this matters

Granola bars are the travel snack of childhood — stroller bags, car seats, hike pockets — so this word and this break-apart game ride everywhere.

What it teaches

Shape spotting among lookalikes, break-and-count fractions, and travel-snack patience.

Words to learn

granola baroatsbreaklinespiecespocket

Say this to your child

“Find the granola bar — the long bumpy one! See the lines? It wants to break there. Press... snap! How many pieces? Two! Eat one... how many now? One! The pocket picnic shares itself.”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and hunt its bumps — oats! raisins! — then find the long lines where the bar wants to break. Give the child a real bar, find the lines with one finger, and press-snap: how many pieces? Count them. Eat one, count again. Finish by asking where the bar likes to travel — pockets, bags, hikes.

Look closer at the picture

Watch the break: some children snap clean on the line, some crush gloriously. Both outcomes count — the crush becomes crumbled granola over yogurt, which is also a lesson.

Ask your child

Where is the granola bar? Where does it want to break? How many pieces now? Where does it like to travel?

What your child can say or do

Long one! / Snap! / Two pieces. / In my pocket.

Out in the real world

Granola bars live in every stroller organizer and hike pack — the break-and-count works on trails, in cars and at every waiting room.

Try it together

Trail pack: deal five snack cards and let the child pack only the travel snacks — bar, crackers, fruit — into a paper bag for the pretend hike. Pack, hike around the rug, unpack and count the haul.

Understanding check

Ask what a granola bar is made of. Oats, bumps, honey, or a finger-traced line — all pass.

This lesson pairs with the Granola Bar flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Cafeteria.

CAFETERIA LESSON · CAFETERIA · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Grapes — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the grapes card as the deck’s prettiest cluster — pointed at, counted in threes, and served with the one safety rule that matters.

Download the card ↓

Open the full lesson

What is this?

Grapes grow in bunches: dozens of round balls hanging from one curly stem, purple or green. Each grape is its own fruit, and the bunch is the family they arrive in.

What does it mean?

Point to the grapes is the pointing drill — but the bunch adds a bonus: pointing at one grape inside a crowd of grapes trains finger precision, not just pointing.

What does the child need to know?

Safety first, always: whole grapes are a choking risk at this age. Cut them lengthwise, every time, before any counting game starts.

Why this matters

Grapes ride in every lunchbox and every fruit bowl — the bunch picture also quietly teaches the set idea: many grapes, one stem, one bunch.

What it teaches

Precise pointing within a cluster, counting in threes, and food-safety awareness.

Words to learn

grapesbunchstempurplecountcut

Say this to your child

“A whole bunch of grapes — and every one is its own ball! Point to just one... there! Now count three: one, two, three. Three for you — snip snip, cut small — and three for me. Trade! Now how many?”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and point to the whole bunch, then to one single grape inside it — one finger, one grape. Count three grapes aloud, touching each. Then serve real grapes — cut lengthwise, every one — and count three into a cup: three for you, three for me. Trade one back and forth and recount after each trade.

Look closer at the picture

Watch the single-grape point: landing on one ball inside the bunch takes aim, and the aim improves visibly within a single session.

Ask your child

Where is one grape? How many did we count? What color is the bunch? What do we do to grapes before eating?

What your child can say or do

One grape! / Purple balls! / Three! / Cut small.

Out in the real world

Grapes arrive in bunches at every market — the bunch picture is also the child’s first diagram of a family: many balls, one stem, all connected.

Try it together

Grape shop: count grapes into tiny cups — orders of three, four, five — and serve the cups to stuffed customers. Cut small, count loud, serve proud.

Understanding check

Ask what we always do to grapes before eating. Cut them, cut small, snip lengthwise — any safety answer passes the check.

This lesson pairs with the Grapes flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Cafeteria.
